summary: Richard Watson of the Network Information Center proposes a compromise for naming hosts: a formal name made of an institution and a host or station part, plus optional nicknames. He lists the requirements any scheme must meet, as earlier proposals had not been accepted.

plainLanguage.summary: After many arguments over computer nicknames, the information office suggests everyone gets a formal name and may also keep a favorite nickname.

subtitle: A 1971 proposal from the NIC for formal host names plus optional nicknames, to settle the naming argument.

tldr.problem: People held strong feelings about host names, and no earlier proposal, including RFC 247, had been accepted.
tldr.mechanism: Each host gets a formal name of the form institution mnemonic, a dash and a host or NIC station mnemonic, with an optional nickname. Hosts choose their own names through their liaison.
tldr.outcome: The author asked liaisons to send their names by November 5 and said the NIC was the logical place to handle the matter. It obsoletes RFC 237.

today: RFC 273 obsoletes RFC 237 and builds on RFC 247. Its metadata does not record it as obsoleted.

sections.title: What Any Scheme Must Do
sections.content: The author says the NIC is a logical place to handle the problem and that the subject is delicate. Any naming scheme must recognize the expanding network, which might eventually have several hundred sites, the need for abbreviations that are easy to type, the use of names in hardcopy and online documentation, and people's strong identification with historical project names.
sections.plainLanguage: A good naming plan has to work when the network gets much bigger, be short to type, and respect the names people already love.

sections.title: Formal Names and Nicknames
sections.content:
Each host has a formal name made of an institution mnemonic, a dash and a host or NIC station mnemonic, and an optional nickname. The institution mnemonic is at most 4 characters, formed as in RFC 247, such as AMES, CASE or UCLA.

The second part has no length limit but should be short. The suggested priority is a suborganization, then a project mnemonic, then a machine designation, and the TIP or TEST designation from RFC 247 should probably be kept. The nickname should be unique across the network and preferably equal to the host mnemonic. The author strongly recommends that Telnets recognize both the formal name and the nickname.
sections.plainLanguage: A formal name says where a computer is and which one it is. A nickname is a short pet name that should match.

sections.title: Who Chooses and What Happens Next
sections.content:
The only satisfactory answer to who picks the names is that hosts choose their own through their liaison, possibly after discussion if duplicate or very long names appear. Hosts at one institution should share the same institution mnemonic.

The author hoped to settle the issue by November 5 and asked each liaison to send names by then. Any implementation hardship cases, other than TIPs, should be reported.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer's own helper chooses its name. Everyone at one place uses the same place code, and the answers were due by a set date.

references.text: Karp, P., Proffered set of standard host names, RFC 247.
